SEC13A-01.note: Second clause has a noun-clause subject ('how the animals tell ... ') with verb 'remained' far downstream; needs comma + coordinator. B comma splice; C 'though' makes the post-semicolon part a dependent clause (fragment) - strongest distractor; D 'in how' leaves 'remained' subjectless. Answering requires finding 'remained', which is the real difficulty. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct.

SEC13A-02.note: 'reveal [to anyone familiar ... impressions] [how many ...]' - verb + indirect-object phrase + noun-clause object; no punctuation between. A (single comma before object) is the strong distractor because the long to-phrase feels like it wants a pause and is not comma-opened. C fragment, D 'and how' has nothing to coordinate with. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct, incl. the D reading as a second object of 'with'.

SEC13A-03.note: After the blank: 'until X were introduced, photographers ... had to carry' is a full independent clause; joining it to the opening independent clause needs comma + FANBOYS. Only C supplies a coordinator, so a student who checks for comma+FANBOYS gets it without much parsing (option-set tell). A comma splice (strongest, reads as until modifying 'dried'); B run-on; D 'even' is not a coordinator. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct. Flag: key is the only option carrying a coordinating conjunction, so comma+FANBOYS recognition picks it without locating the second clause; keep only if the hard route tolerates that.

SEC13A-04.note: Dash after 'revealed' opens the interrupter 'once the dark varnish ... was lifted'; must close with a dash. Dash-pairing glance kills A, B, C. A is the strongest because the interrupter contains its own comma pair. Standard paired-dash item, length is the only difficulty. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct. Paired-dash glance item; medium, not hard.

SEC13A-05.note: 'make one pattern unmistakable: [the pattern as an independent clause]'. A comma splice (strongest, intro-phrase 'in nearly every season ...' disguises it); C fuses 'in nearly every season' into the first clause and splices 'the hives gained'; D 'which' clause has no verb of its own. 'one pattern' cues the colon. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct (calling C a 'comma splice' is loose - it is a splice at the later comma - but the path produces the key).

SEC13A-06.note: Two independent clauses ('The researchers traced ... trackway' / 'they identified ...'), second fronted by a long prepositional phrase. Semicolon. A comma splice (strongest); B run-on reading 'beside' as modifying 'meters'; D 'beside which' makes a relative clause but then 'they identified' leaves 'which' dangling - borderline, but the main subject 'they' after a relative 'which' is ungrammatical. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct.

SEC13B-01.note: Subject 'The fossil teeth that ... dug from an eroding riverbank over a single wet summer in the 1980s' + verb 'ultimately settled'. No punctuation. C (single comma between relative clause and its own adverbial, i.e., inside the subject) is strong after the dash-pair interrupter; A unpaired dash; B 'which' steals 'settled' and leaves 'teeth' without a verb. Need to locate the main verb 'settled'. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct. Best of the no-punctuation items.

SEC13B-02.note: After the existing semicolon the clause is 'when researchers gave it to mice, whose livers ... fragments, [however,] the antiviral effect ... vanished' - subordinate clause + nonrestrictive relative needing its closing comma + main clause. 'however' sits as an interrupting adverb between them, so commas on both sides. A (the trained '; however,' reflex) leaves 'when ... fragments' as a fragment between two semicolons - strongest distractor; B fragment sentence; D fragment before semicolon. Inverts the usual however rule - genuinely hard. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct. Strongest item in the batch: the trained '; however,' reflex is the trap.

SEC13B-03.note: Closing dash after 'poisoning' requires an opening dash before the appositive 'three chemicals ...'. Dash pairing settles it at a glance. C comma is the only tempting one (comma-dash mismatch). Same wet-plate photography topic as SEC13A-03 - topical duplication in one batch. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct. Drop for the hard route: the closing dash after 'poisoning' settles it at a glance (easy), and it repeats SEC13A-03's wet-collodion photography topic and ten-minute detail in the same batch.

SEC13B-04.note: Statement then a direct question ('Why ... did they leave ...?'), inverted with a question mark: new sentence. B comma splice of question onto statement (strongest); C run-on; D 'asking why ... did they ... ?' indirect question cannot keep inversion and '?'. The final '?' plus inverted 'did they' strike C/D quickly. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct. Medium; the final '?' and inversion are visible tells.

SEC13B-05.note: 'a membrane protein that [in the presence of ... tear] rapidly gathers at the breach' - restrictive relative clause with a long interposed prepositional phrase. C/D make 'In the presence of the calcium ions admitted through a tear rapidly gathers' a subjectless clause - strong because 'admitted ... rapidly gathers' looks like it could have 'ions' as subject; B 'and' coordinate clause has no subject. Must notice 'gathers' needs 'that' as its subject. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct.

SEC13B-06.note: Appositive 'a former apprentice ... when he quit the workshop' opened by a comma after 'printer' must close with a comma before the direct object 'the exclusive right'. Comma-pairing glance strikes B (dash) and A (period); C is the strongest (no close), helped by the internal 'according to one hostile pamphlet' comma pair. PHASE 2: Key matches; explanation correct. Comma-pair matching item; medium.
